headline: Multiple crude bomb blasts hit Dhaka, leaving at least 2 injured
summary: Explosions were reported in Babubazar, Moghbazar, Rampura, and New Market on Thursday evening and night.
details: At least two people were injured after a crude bomb exploded under the Babubazar Bridge in Dhaka on Thursday evening.
The injured individuals, identified as Mosharraf Hossain (42) and Abdur Rashid (38) from Munshiganj, were hurt around 7:54 PM, according to Kotwali Police Station.
Similar blasts were reported in other parts of the city, including a crude bomb explosion at the Moghbazar intersection, though no injuries were reported there.
Later around 11:00 PM, two more crude bombs exploded on the road opposite BTV Bhaban in Rampura, with no casualties reported.
Another explosion occurred in front of Dhaka College in the New Market area late last night, according to New Market Police Station officials.
Police are currently investigating the incidents to determine the exact timing and the number of explosive devices used in the New Market blast.
caption:
Crude bomb blasts rocked several parts of Dhaka on Thursday, leaving at least two people injured.

At least two people were injured after a crude bomb exploded under the Babubazar Bridge in Dhaka on Thursday evening.

The injured individuals, identified as Mosharraf Hossain (42) and Abdur Rashid (38) from Munshiganj, were hurt around 7:54 PM, according to Kotwali Police Station.

Similar blasts were reported in other parts of the city, including a crude bomb explosion at the Moghbazar intersection, though no injuries were reported there.

Later around 11:00 PM, two more crude bombs exploded on the road opposite BTV Bhaban in Rampura, with no casualties reported.

Another explosion occurred in front of Dhaka College in the New Market area late last night, according to New Market Police Station officials.

Police are currently investigating the incidents to determine the exact timing and the number of explosive devices used in the New Market blast.

headline_marked: 23,301 cases in 18 days: [[Dengue outbreak could peak in October]]
headline: 23,301 cases in 18 days: Dengue outbreak could peak in October
summary: Experts warn of a surge in infections and deaths as continued rainfall creates ideal breeding conditions for mosquitoes.
details: According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), dengue cases reached 23,301 in the first 18 days of September, a significant increase from 20,536 in August and 9,206 in July.
Deaths have also risen sharply, with 79 reported so far this month, compared with 43 in August and 36 in July.
Professor Kabirul Bashar of Jahangirnagar University warns that the outbreak could peak in October because continued rainfall provides ideal conditions for mosquito breeding.
Bashar noted a 45-60 day lag between rainfall and its impact on transmission, meaning September rains could drive cases up through October.
Entomologist GM Saifur Rahman suggests that eliminating breeding sites alone is no longer enough and calls for the identification of "red clusters" to intensify control efforts.
Rahman advocates for a dedicated central body to oversee surveillance, monitor virus serotypes, and track mosquito populations to ensure accountability.
To increase community engagement, Rahman proposes neighborhood-level incentives, such as designating "Mosquito-Free Zones" and providing basic control equipment to volunteers.
caption:
23,301 dengue cases in just 18 days. Experts warn the crisis could peak in October.

According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), dengue cases reached 23,301 in the first 18 days of September, a significant increase from 20,536 in August and 9,206 in July.

Deaths have also risen sharply, with 79 reported so far this month, compared with 43 in August and 36 in July.

Professor Kabirul Bashar of Jahangirnagar University warns that the outbreak could peak in October because continued rainfall provides ideal conditions for mosquito breeding.

Bashar noted a 45-60 day lag between rainfall and its impact on transmission, meaning September rains could drive cases up through October.

Entomologist GM Saifur Rahman suggests that eliminating breeding sites alone is no longer enough and calls for the identification of "red clusters" to intensify control efforts.

Rahman advocates for a dedicated central body to oversee surveillance, monitor virus serotypes, and track mosquito populations to ensure accountability.

To increase community engagement, Rahman proposes neighborhood-level incentives, such as designating "Mosquito-Free Zones" and providing basic control equipment to volunteers.
